Duration (5 months), symptom pattern (post-void relief followed by rapid return), and absence of acute systemic signs strongly favor IC/BPS over acute infection. Chronic bacterial cystitis is plausible given persistent irritative voiding symptoms and dyspareunia, though typically associated with recurrent positive cultures—less likely without documented prior UTIs or risk factors (e.g., neurogenic bladder, stones). Urethral syndrome overlaps clinically and may represent a subset of IC/BPS or early-stage disease; included separately due to distinct diagnostic criteria (urethral tenderness, sterile urine, no cystoscopic Hunner lesions). Vulvodynia with pelvic floor involvement commonly coexists with IC/BPS and can refer pain to the bladder and cause secondary bladder symptoms and dyspareunia—especially relevant given the absence of objective urologic findings on history alone. Bladder adenocarcinoma is rare (<2% of bladder cancers) but must be considered in chronic, progressive irritative symptoms refractory to standard therapy; however, lack of hematuria, age, or risk factors (e.g., smoking, chemical exposure) lowers pretest probability—hence lowest confidence. Diagnostic uncertainty is moderately high due to clinical overlap among chronic pelvic pain syndromes and need for cystoscopy with hydrodistension and/or biopsy to confirm IC/BPS or rule out malignancy."}
